title: When is Claude Haiku good enough? It depends on how many steps your task has
body_markdown:
Published coding benchmarks put[Claude Haiku 4.5](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-haiku-4-5) within about 6 points of Sonnet 4.6: 73.3% on[SWE-bench verified](https://www.swebench.com/) against 79.6%, at a third of the price. Read that, and the obvious move is to default to the cheap tier and escalate when something fails.


We ran both tiers over our own suite of enterprise automation tasks, which span building, operating, and diagnosing real UiPath projects. The suite is open source and lives in[UiPath/skills](https://github.com/UiPath/skills/tree/main/tests) , with one YAML file per task, if you want to see what the work looks like. Same 400+ tasks, same harness, same day, neither run reusing cached results. Haiku 4.5 passed 42.0%. Sonnet 4.6 passed 85.6%.


The same two models both times. Both numbers are honestly measured, so the interesting question is not which one is right. It is why they disagree this much and what the second measures that the first does not.


### The two measurements are not measuring the same work


The story that suggests itself is that benchmarks test one-shot patches while real work is long chains of steps. It is tidy; we believed it for a while, and it does not hold up. Published[SWE-agent](https://swe-agent.com/) trajectories run to tens of tool calls, and our own median task takes 22 commands, so on raw step count the two regimes look broadly comparable.


What the step count hides is that a step is not the same unit in both places. A SWE-bench instance is graded on a patch, usually a small one, applied to a repository that already builds and runs; most of the trajectory goes into locating where that small change belongs. **The trajectory is long, but the change it produces is small.** Our tasks are graded on what the agent produced, and across the suite that ranges from projects scaffolded and packaged from nothing, through workflows wired across several services, to configuration that has to be exactly right for a later step to work at all. Comparable step counts, but far more of those steps are building something rather than locating something.


A second difference runs alongside it. **On one side the agent can check its own work, and on the other it cannot.** SWE-bench resolution means hidden tests pass, and the agent has the repository’s own tests to run in the meantime. Anthropic’s[published scaffold](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/swe-bench-sonnet) builds the loop into the prompt: step 2 is “create a script to reproduce the error and execute it,” and step 4 is “rerun your reproduce script and confirm that the error is fixed.” A wrong step gets caught and repaired inside the task. Our grader executes checks the agent never sees: a hidden checker script, a debug run, and a validator pointed at a path the agent had to get right, and there is no second attempt. A wrong flag in command 3 is still wrong 40 commands later.


### Every doubling of length halves Haiku’s odds


That leaves the separate question the title asks: within our suite, with the grading regime held fixed, does chain length predict whether the cheap tier finishes?


Two real tasks make “length” concrete. Both are about weather, and both arrive as a plain English request.[The short one](https://github.com/UiPath/skills/blob/bcb7e262bccebe8740871db99ba16f6e2b203935/tests/tasks/uipath-maestro-flow/smoke/init_validate.yaml) :


> *Create a new UiPath Flow project called “WeatherAlert” and make sure it validates successfully.*


Create the enclosing solution, create the flow project inside it, run the validator. That took 7 commands for Sonnet 4.6. Haiku 4.5 passed it too.


[The long one](https://github.com/UiPath/skills/blob/bcb7e262bccebe8740871db99ba16f6e2b203935/tests/tasks/uipath-maestro-flow/multi_node/slack_weather_pipeline/slack_weather_pipeline.yaml) :


> *Create a flow called “SlackWeatherPipeline”. Read the #office-bellevue Slack channel description to find out which city the office is in, then fetch the current weather for that city from open-meteo. If it’s above 60F output ‘warm office today’, otherwise ‘cold office today’.*


Nothing there is conceptually harder. But the finished artifact is a 5-node graph with data flowing through it: a Slack connector into a script that extracts the city, into an HTTP call, into a decision on the 60F threshold, into an end node, and it has to survive both the validator and a debug run that actually executes. That took 65 commands for Sonnet 4.6, which passed. Haiku 4.5 earned 38% of the weighted credit and did not finish.


**Same domain, same skill, same grader, roughly a 10x difference in how much has to go right.** That is the axis this post is about, and across the suite it separates the two tiers cleanly. We measure length on the **Sonnet 4.6** run since a failing model thrashes and its own step count then reflects the failure rather than the task.


Haiku 4.5 declines monotonically across all 6 bands, from 89.5% down to 21.2%. Sonnet 4.6 gives up 11 points over the same range. The most useful fact here sits at the left edge: **on short tasks of 1 or 2 commands, Haiku 4.5 matches Sonnet 4.6 exactly, 89.5% each.** Pay for the expensive tier there, and you get nothing for it.


Fit each series on a doubling scale, and Haiku 4.5 loses 13.6 points of pass rate per doubling of task length, against 2.8 for Sonnet 4.6. A logistic fit on individual tasks, so the band boundaries cannot be doing the work, gives the same answer: **every doubling of task length roughly halves Haiku 4.5’s odds of finishing** (p = 3 × 10⁻¹⁸ across 408 tasks), where Sonnet 4.6’s decline is real but far shallower, and the two slopes differ significantly (p = 0.013). Length alone separates the outcomes well enough that if you pick one task Haiku passed and one it failed, it tells you which was which about 3 times in 4.


The controls hold. Splitting each task family at its own median command count keeps the effect, at 57.2% against 31.5%, and stripping infrastructure failures and turn caps moves Haiku only to 45.6%.


The mechanism is presumably error compounding. If a model gets each step right with probability p, an n-step task finishes only if every step lands, which happens with probability pⁿ, a product and not a sum. **A per-step difference too small to notice becomes a finishing difference too large to miss:** 99% and 97% per-step reliability are nearly indistinguishable over 3 steps, 97% against 91%, and diverge to 67% and 30% by step 40.


METR’s[time-horizon work](https://metr.org/time-horizons/) reaches the same conclusion from a different direction. Instead of counting an agent’s steps, they measure how long a task takes a human expert, then find the duration at which a model succeeds half the time, its 50% time horizon. Task length predicts success at R² = 0.83. The figure we find most useful is a second one: their 80% horizon runs about 5 times shorter than the 50% horizon, so Claude 3.7 Sonnet succeeded half the time on tasks that take a human about an hour but reached 80% reliability only on 15-minute ones. **Raising the reliability bar shortens the task you can trust** , which is our result in their units, arrived at with no machinery in common.


### Doing this on your own, Coder Eval runs


Both runs came out of[Coder Eval](https://github.com/UiPath/coder_eval) , the open-source harness we use for this. It runs a real coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, or Gemini/Antigravity) in a sandbox against declarative YAML tasks, then grades the files and the commands the agent actually produced. A task is one YAML file, and getting started looks like this:


```text
pip install coder-eval  coder-eval run tasks/hello_date.yaml  coder-eval report runs/latest
```


Swap the model, point it at your own tasks, and the rest is bookkeeping. Here is[the short weather task](https://github.com/UiPath/skills/blob/bcb7e262bccebe8740871db99ba16f6e2b203935/tests/tasks/uipath-maestro-flow/smoke/init_validate.yaml) from earlier, abridged to two of its five criteria:


```text
task_id: skill-flow-init-validate  tags: [uipath-maestro-flow, smoke, lifecycle:generate]   run_limits:    expected_turns: 9   initial_prompt: |    Create a new UiPath Flow project called "WeatherAlert" and make sure it    validates successfully.   success_criteria:    - type: command_executed      description: "Agent initialized a Flow project with uip maestro flow init"      tool_name: "Bash"      command_pattern: '(uip|\$UIP)\s+(maestro\s+)?flow\s+init'      weight: 1.5      pass_threshold: 1.0     - type: file_exists      description: "Flow file was created inside the solution"      path: "WeatherAlert/WeatherAlert/WeatherAlert.flow"      weight: 1.5      pass_threshold: 1.0
```


Every run then writes a single run.json, and each task result in it already carries its own step counts as a side effect of normal execution. Here is that same task from the Sonnet 4.6 run, abridged:


```text
{    "task_id": "skill-flow-init-validate",    "status": "SUCCESS",    "actual_commands": 7,    "iterations": [      { "iteration": 1, "command_count": 7, "assistant_turn_count": 13, "crashed": false }    ]  }
```


That is 7 commands, the figure quoted for this task earlier. That is where every chain length in this post came from: no transcript parsing, no new fields, no rerun. **Once the runs exist, reanalyzing them comprehensively is cheap** , and a month of nightly runs across two model tiers already has a result like this sitting on disk.


### In short: the tiers converge on short tasks and diverge on long ones


On 1 or 2 commands of work, Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 4.6 both pass 89.5%, and past 40 commands, Haiku finishes 1 task in 5, whereas Sonnet finishes 4, with every doubling of length in between roughly halving its odds. The same two tiers sit 6 points apart on SWE-bench Verified and 44 apart on our suite, where the benchmark asks for a small change to code that already works and lets the agent test it while our tasks ask for a whole artifact and grade it once, unseen. A model-tier comparison looks like a question about the models. It is first a question about how long your tasks are.


### References

- Anthropic, **“Claude Sonnet 4.6 System Card”** — Table 2.1.A. Source for 79.6% on SWE-bench Verified, run with adaptive thinking at max effort and default sampling settings.[https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-4-6-system-card](https://www.anthropic.com/claude-sonnet-4-6-system-card)
- Anthropic Engineering, **“Raising the bar on SWE-bench Verified with Claude 3.5 Sonnet”** — the two-tool scaffold, and the reproduce-then-rerun prompt steps quoted above.[https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/swe-bench-sonnet](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/swe-bench-sonnet)
- **SWE-bench** (Jimenez, Yang et al., ICLR 2024) — the benchmark and its Verified subset.[https://www.swebench.com/](https://www.swebench.com/)
- OpenAI, **“Introducing SWE-bench Verified”** (Aug 2024) — the human-filtered 500-instance subset that leaderboards report on.[https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/](https://openai.com/index/introducing-swe-bench-verified/)
- **SWE-agent** (John Yang et al., 2024) — the agent-computer-interface scaffold whose published trajectories run to tens of tool calls per instance.[https://swe-agent.com/](https://swe-agent.com/)
- METR, **“Task-Completion Time Horizons of Frontier AI Models”** — the 50% time-horizon methodology and the running measurements.[https://metr.org/time-horizons/](https://metr.org/time-horizons/) — the R² = 0.83 length-vs-success fit and the 50% and 80% horizon figures are from the underlying paper, *Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks* (Mar 2025).[https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.14499)
